item.title: 30 years of cross-provincial effort transform Minning in China's Ningxia
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
VistaNingxia | 30 years of cross-provincial effort transform Minning in China's Ningxia-Xinhua VistaNingxia | 30 years of cross-provincial effort transform Minning in China's Ningxia Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-16 16:10:17 An aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 11, 2026 shows a view of Minning Town in Yongning County of Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen) YINCHUAN, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Located in the east of the Helan Mountains, Minning Town, named after the Chinese abbreviations of Fujian and Ningxia, stands as a living testament to China's poverty alleviation efforts, where a deserted land was turned into a new homeland for over 60,000 people. In 1996, when the east-west poverty alleviation collaboration was carried out, southeast China's Fujian Province was designated to provide pairing assistance to northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. In 1997, construction began on Minning Village on barren land near Yinchuan, the regional capital. Later, officials from Fujian Province came here in batches to take part in the construction, along with assisting funds and projects. The cross-provincial effort transformed Minning into a modern town, with a population rising from some 8,000 to over 60,000, mainly living on growing wine grapes, mushrooms, and goji berries and raising cattle. item.title: Chinese Gravity-1 rocket launches new satellites from sea
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
A Gravity-1 Y3 carrier rocket carrying nine satellites blasts off from waters off the coast of Shanghai in east China on Sept. 16, 2026. The launch mission was carried out by the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center. The satellites, a new group of Qianfan Constellation satellites and an EUHT technology test satellite, lifted off at 6 a.m. (Beijing Time) atop a Gravity-1 Y3 carrier rocket. The mission was declared a complete success. (Photo by Zhang Shuo/Xinhua) SHANGHAI, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China launched nine satellites into preset orbits on Wednesday from waters off the coast of Shanghai in east China. The Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center carried out the launch mission. The satellites, a new group of Qianfan Constellation satellites and an EUHT technology test satellite, lifted off at 6 a.m. (Beijing Time) atop a Gravity-1 Y3 carrier rocket. The mission was declared a complete success. The mission set new records for China's single sea launch in terms of payload weight and orbital altitude, with a net payload weight of over three tonnes and an insertion altitude of about 800 kilometers, verifying the sea launch model's adaptability to medium- and large-sized satellite payload missions, according to the Chinese commercial aerospace company OrienSpace, the developer of the rocket. The Gravity-1 rocket has carried out four sea launches so far, all of which were successful. Today's mission marked Gravity-1's first launch for the networking of a large low-Earth-orbit satellite internet constellation. According to OrienSpace, the satellites aboard the rocket were manufactured in Shanghai and launched from waters near Shanghai. Such land-sea coordination helps improve the overall efficiency of both commercial space manufacturing and launch operations. ■ A Gravity-1 Y3 carrier rocket carrying nine satellites blasts off from waters off the coast of Shanghai in east China on Sept. 16, 2026. item.title: China opens major river-to-sea canal, creating trade shortcut to Southeast Asia
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
A cargo vessel prepares to depart for Yangpu Port in south China's Hainan Province along the Pinglu Canal at an operation area in Nanning Port, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 16, 2026. China opened a major new canal on Wednesday, giving its landlocked southwest a shortcut to the coast and overseas markets, particularly those in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the country's largest trading partner. Built at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan (about 10.75 billion U.S. dollars), the 134.2-kilometer Pinglu Canal runs from Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming) NANNING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China opened the Pinglu Canal on Wednesday, giving its landlocked southwest a shortcut to the coast and overseas markets, particularly those in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the country's largest trading partner. Built at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan (about 10.75 billion U.S. dollars), the 134.2-kilometer canal runs from Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China. The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. It is the first river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from southwest China to the sea by more than 560 kilometers compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong Province. It is expected to reduce overall logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent and save more than 5 billion yuan in transportation costs each year. Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi, said the canal creates a new link between China's market of 1.4 billion people and ASEAN's nearly 700 million consumers. Its impact, Lu said, could extend beyond the movement of goods, spurring new cross-border investment and deepening regional supply-chain integration. The canal took over four years to build. Most of it was created by widening, deepening and straightening existing waterways, while a small section had to be excavated through dry land and mountainous terrain. One of the biggest engineering challenges was a 65-meter difference in water level, roughly the height of a 20-plus-story building. Three navigation hubs, all featuring twin-line ship locks, were built to raise and lower vessels along the canal. Environmental protection was another priority during construction. More than 98 percent of the roughly 315 million cubic meters of earth and rock excavated during construction was reused. The canal also includes a fish passage more than 480 meters long and a dedicated wildlife crossing for land animals including leopard cats and squirrels. The canal opens in the first year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), as the world's second-largest economy seeks to promote more coordinated regional development and further expand high-standard opening up -- priorities outlined in the plan. The new artery carries particular significance for China's southwest, which has long lagged behind the more prosperous eastern coast and faced higher costs getting goods to seaports. Coal, ore, grain, new-energy materials and auto parts from the region can now take a more direct route to overseas markets. China's trade with ASEAN exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars for the first time last year. In the first seven months of 2026, total trade between the two sides reached 744.41 billion U.S. dollars, an increase of 24.7 percent year on year, accounting for 21.8 percent of China's total foreign trade during this period. For Boonsub Panichakarn from the Faculty of Logistics and Digital Supply Chain at Naresuan University in Thailand, the canal's significance goes beyond the distance it saves. It lies in how much the canal can reduce logistics costs, time variability and uncertainty across the entire ASEAN-southwest China supply chain, he said. ■ A cargo vessel prepares to depart for Yangpu Port in south China's Hainan Province along the Pinglu Canal, in Nanning Port, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 16, 2026. item.title: Hong Kong unveils 1st five-year plan for economic, social development
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
HONG KONG, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) unveiled its first five-year plan for economic and social development (2026-2030) on Wednesday. The first five-year plan for economic and social development (2026-2030) will help build a more open, inclusive, liberal, prosperous and safer Hong Kong, John Lee, chief executive of the HKSAR, said on Wednesday. Unveiling the blueprint, Lee said the 2026-2030 period is five crucial years for Hong Kong to seize the opportunity to expedite the transition from stability to prosperity, enhance social well-being, and build a better home for all. Hong Kong will consolidate and enhance its status as an international financial, maritime and trade center, and develop itself into an international I&T center and a global hub for high-caliber talent, thus sharpening its competitive edge, according to the plan. Efforts will also be made to expedite the development of the Northern Metropolis, deepen the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and create an international collaboration network. The plan also vows to enhance social well-being and refine the social protection framework. Noting that this year marks the beginning of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), Lee said that the inaugural blueprint represents a major initiative by the HKSAR government to uphold and enhance the executive-led system and improve governance efficacy. The blueprint signaled the strategic planning need for Hong Kong to proactively align with national development strategies and better integrate into and serve the overall national development, the chief executive added. ■

item.title: China issues world's first medical-device standard for AI-powered brain-computer interfaces
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China has approved and issued the country's third medical-device standard for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), which is also the world's first such standard for BCI medical devices using artificial intelligence (AI) to process electroencephalogram (EEG) data. BCI technology establishes a direct communication route between the brains of humans or animals and external devices. By capturing and decoding neural signals, BCI enables seamless interaction between brain and machine, ultimately allowing control over assistive devices to execute intended actions. China's BCI sector is accelerating its transition from the laboratory to industrialization, making steady progress via the market launch of diverse related products and thanks to surging investment in the sector. The standard, issued by the National Medical Products Administration, specifies quality requirements and evaluation methods for EEG datasets used by AI algorithms in BCI medical devices. It applies to datasets used in research and development, production, quality control and other stages of BCI medical device technology that uses AI algorithms to post-process EEG signals. The standard covers requirements for the collection, processing, annotation, storage and access of EEG data, as well as methods for testing dataset quality. It will help address common industry challenges, including inconsistent quality-control criteria and non-standardized dataset development. The administration said AI-powered BCIs depend on large and high-quality EEG datasets to train algorithms to decode brain signals and identify patients' intentions. In medical applications, the quality and consistency of such data can directly affect the performance and safety of the devices. To support major innovations in BCI medical devices and meet the urgent needs of the industry, the administration adopted an expedited procedure for the development and approval of this standard. China previously issued two BCI medical-device standards in 2025, covering terminology and test methods for the sensing and response performance of implantable neural stimulators with closed-loop functions. The new standard will take effect on Sept. 1, 2027. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- A red light once posed a routine dilemma for China's food delivery riders -- stop and risk an overdue delivery that could directly affect earnings, or press on to beat the countdown ticking away on their phones. For Li Yipeng, a rider in Suzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, that trade-off is now coming into play less. His delivery app now records the time he spends waiting at red lights and adds it back to his delivery window, reflecting a wider effort to make the algorithms governing more than 10 million delivery riders take safety, rather than efficiency alone, into account. "We can clearly see how long we have waited and how much time has been added back," Li said. "There is no need to run red lights anymore." The "red-light clock stop" mechanism, first launched in parts of Suzhou in late July, was later pledged by Meituan, Taobao Flash Sale and JD Takeaway for future trials in parts of Beijing. It is among a series of recent changes to delivery algorithms, alongside broader exemptions for delays beyond riders' control and efforts to make platform rules more transparent. "Algorithms cannot calculate efficiency while leaving humanity out," said Zhao Lei, a senior researcher with the Meituan Research Institute, on the latest episode of China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency. Apart from the red-light mechanism, platforms such as Meituan have also introduced penalty exemptions for late deliveries caused by extreme weather and abnormal road conditions. Zhao said such measures use technology to give riders more time and ease their anxiety over delivery deadlines. Other cities are seeking to give riders more time by removing obstacles during the final leg of a delivery. In north China's Tianjin Municipality, a digital access system was introduced, allowing delivery riders to enter residential compounds with their scooters after identity verification. JD delivery rider Zhai Zhongguo said that in some compounds where delivery vehicles were previously barred from entering, riders had to leave their scooters outside and continue on foot. "It used to take at least 20 minutes to walk in, make the delivery and walk back out," he said. For riders whose delivery time is calculated by the minute, a community gate can disrupt a string of subsequent orders. To further ease riders' time pressure, the platforms have also reduced or removed penalties for delayed deliveries and begun showing consumers estimated delivery windows rather than a single precise arrival time, according to China's cyberspace regulator. Greater flexibility has been accompanied by efforts to make the algorithms themselves less opaque. Zhao said Meituan has conducted 11 rounds of algorithm disclosure, explaining to riders how orders are assigned, prices set, and how rewards and penalties are determined. Such changes by platforms, together with measures introduced by Chinese cities, have been unfolding under a broader national policy framework aimed at strengthening protections for workers in new forms of employment, including delivery riders, ride-hailing drivers, truck drivers, online marketers, livestreamers and domestic-service workers. A detailed set of guidelines made public in April by the Chinese government calls on internet platforms to regulate algorithms, improve transparency, and protect workers' rights to be informed about, participate in and choose algorithm-related rules. They also require platforms to hear views from trade unions and worker representatives when adjusting rules on order allocation, pricing and delivery-time estimates. The guidelines also call for a social security system better suited to the characteristics of these workers, including expanding occupational injury protection and improving mechanisms for transferring social insurance accounts. In northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, 24-year-old delivery rider Cai Daizhu suffered a traffic accident less than a month after starting the job, injuring a ligament in his right knee and spending nearly half a year recovering. He recently learned that he was entitled to about 28,000 yuan (about 4,140 U.S. dollars) in occupational injury benefits, while eligible follow-up medical and rehabilitation expenses could also be reimbursed. Cai's case shows how occupational injury protection in China is adapting to new forms of employment. Traditional work injury insurance generally requires an established employment relationship, while many delivery riders work across multiple platforms or move frequently between jobs. The new scheme instead links coverage to whether an injury occurs while a worker is carrying out a platform order, and riders themselves do not pay. The scheme has expanded substantially since its pilot launch in 2022. From July 1 this year, it was rolled out nationwide, with participating platform companies increasing to 25. By the end of July, the number of people enrolled in this scheme had reached 34.59 million. Protection is also expanding beyond occupational injuries. JD pays the full cost of the five major social insurance programs, namely pension, medical, unemployment, work injury and maternity insurance, and the housing provident fund for its full-time delivery riders. Meituan subsidizes pension insurance contributions for eligible riders, while Taobao Flash Sale provides pension and medical insurance subsidies for eligible riders. At the national level, China is moving to expand social insurance coverage for more workers. The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security said in July that it would encourage and support those in new forms of employment to join the basic pension insurance scheme. The expanded protection is already giving peace of mind to some riders. Li Yan, a full-time JD delivery rider, said signing a labor contract with the company and receiving full coverage under the five social insurance programs and the housing provident fund had "eased worries while working on the road." Highlighting the increasingly important role workers in new forms of employment play in promoting consumption, safeguarding people's livelihoods and stabilizing expectations, Zhao stressed the need to provide them with better support and protection. "They are not only 'connectors' of a better life, but also 'carriers of a city's warmth,'" he said. ■

item.title: Xi congratulates Jilin University on 80th founding anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday sent a congratulatory letter to Jilin University, celebrating its 80th founding anniversary. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, extended congratulations to the faculty, students and alumni of the university. He urged the university to carry forward the revolutionary traditions, leverage its comprehensive strengths, focus on the country's strategic needs, cultivate more high-caliber talent, and make greater contributions to the full revitalization of the Northeast in the new era and to advancing Chinese modernization. ■

item.title: Xi Story: Making canals channels for connectivity, prosperity, better life
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
NANNING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Sitting in a glass case at a museum in south China's Qinzhou, a glazed porcelain bowl etched with a floral pattern offers a tantalizing clue to this coastal city's maritime-trade past. Despite being centuries old, the bowl bears scarcely any signs of use. Experts believe that the bowl, instead of being made for use in local households, was likely among the merchandise stockpiled for trade during the Song Dynasty (960-1279), when sugar and ceramics were shipped from Qinzhou to Southeast Asian countries along the Maritime Silk Road. A historic port city on the coast of the Beibu Gulf in the South China Sea, Qinzhou, located in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, is gaining fresh momentum as a maritime hub with the opening of the Pinglu Canal, a major river-to-sea canal project set to become operational on Wednesday. The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. During an inspection tour of Guangxi in December 2023, Chinese President Xi Jinping was briefed on the construction progress of the canal in front of a sand-table model. Guangxi's future growth potential lies in connecting its waterways to the sea and realizing integrated river-sea transport, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said during that trip. He added that Guangxi should strengthen itself via maritime development, noting that the region has both a strong need and great potential to further expand opening up, both internally and externally. Running from north to south, the Pinglu Canal links the Xijiang River shipping route with the Beibu Gulf. It is expected to shorten the shipping distance between China's southwestern hinterland and ASEAN, China's largest trading partner, by 560 km and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent, according to Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi. China's natural river systems generally run from west to east toward the sea, making it difficult to rely on existing rivers and lakes to connect the country's north and south. China has a long history of building canals. The best-known is the more than 2,500-year-old Grand Canal, the world's oldest and longest artificial waterway system, and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2014. Xi has attached great importance to the protection and revitalization of the Grand Canal. He once stressed that the Grand Canal is a "precious heritage passed down to us by our ancestors." In 2006, when he was secretary of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee, he took a "water bus" along a section of the Grand Canal in the provincial capital Hangzhou to inspect cleanup and revitalization of the canal. The "water bus" passenger service, launched in 2004, was the first of its kind along an urban Grand Canal network. Along the way, Xi asked in detail about everything from waterway network protection and shipping operations to the development of scenic areas along the canal. He encouraged Hangzhou officials to turn the canal into "a canal for the people" and "a canal for visitors," stressing that the people should be the ultimate beneficiaries. His attention to the Grand Canal has remained unchanged over the years. In November 2020, as China's top leader, Xi visited the eastern city of Yangzhou, where some of the waterway system's oldest sections are located. "For centuries, the canal has nourished the cities and people along its banks, bringing prosperity and well-being to them," he said. "I hope everyone will work together to protect the Grand Canal and ensure that it continues to benefit the people for generations to come," he told local officials and residents. Yangzhou, described by Xi as a "wonderful place built along the water, thriving on it and made beautiful by it," is a vivid example of how the Grand Canal has nourished a city and shaped its fortunes. Just like Yangzhou, Qinzhou today is poised to reap the benefits of greater connectivity -- this time, connectivity from river to sea, thanks to the Pinglu Canal. The Pinglu Canal is bringing to life the historical tradition of the Grand Canal in a new era, a tradition of fostering prosperity through waterways, said Xie Zhujun, a researcher with the Guangxi Academy of Social Sciences. Ultimately, the purpose of a canal is to improve people's livelihoods and deliver broader economic and social benefits, he noted. For Ning Qiongri, a Qinzhou native and a vlogger who has posted some 1,600 videos chronicling the construction of the Pinglu Canal, the project promises not only greater prosperity, but also a better life for local people. "Many people find jobs thanks to the canal's construction. I've also seen brand-new villages and schools built along its banks, as well as supermarkets and restaurants that are eager to name themselves after the canal," Ning revealed. ■
